theme: रक्तरंजित लाभ का संकोच / The moral cost of victory
context: After asking how he can fight revered elders Bhishma and Drona, Arjuna explains why he would rather live on alms than gain wealth and enjoyments by killing them. The image of pleasures stained with blood expresses his fear that victory would carry a grave moral and personal cost.
contextHindi: भीष्म और द्रोण जैसे आदरणीय गुरुओं से युद्ध कैसे करें—यह पूछने के बाद अर्जुन अपनी आशंका स्पष्ट करते हैं। वे कहते हैं कि उनसे लड़कर धन और सुख पाने के बजाय भिक्षा पर जीना बेहतर लगेगा। उनके लिए ऐसी जीत के सुख भी रक्त से सने होंगे।
sanskritDevanagari:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्
श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके |
हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव
भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान् ||२-५||
transliteration:
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān śreyo bhoktuṃ bhaikṣyamapīha loke .
hatvārthakāmāṃstu gurūnihaiva bhuñjīya bhogān rudhirapradigdhān ||2-5||

spokenHindi:
अर्जुन अपनी उलझन को और स्पष्ट करते हैं। वे कहते हैं कि जिन गुरुओं का वे आदर करते हैं, उन्हें मारकर जीवन बिताने से बेहतर उन्हें भिक्षा पर जीना लगता है। अगर वे उन्हें मारकर राज्य और सुख पा भी लें, तो वे सुख उन्हें रक्त से सने हुए लगेंगे।

‘रुधिरप्रदिग्धान्’—रक्त से सना हुआ—यहाँ बहुत तीखा चित्र है। अर्जुन केवल जीत की कीमत नहीं गिन रहे; वे पूछ रहे हैं कि जिस सफलता के पीछे प्रिय और पूज्य लोगों की मृत्यु हो, क्या उसे सचमुच सुख कहा जा सकता है? यह उनके मन में करुणा, सम्मान, भय और आसक्ति—इन सबके एक साथ उलझने का क्षण है।

ध्यान रहे, अर्जुन का यह कथन उस महाकाव्य के खास युद्ध-संकट में उनका अपना तर्क है। यह हर कठिन परिस्थिति में जिम्मेदारी छोड़ देने या नुकसानदेह कार्रवाई से बचने का सार्वभौमिक नियम नहीं बन जाता। इस श्लोक का उपयोगी प्रश्न है: क्या कोई उपलब्धि अपने साधनों से नैतिक रूप से दागदार हो सकती है? और जब किसी निर्णय में वास्तविक हानि का डर हो, तो क्या हमें अकेले आवेग में फैसला करने के बजाय विवेकपूर्ण सलाह लेनी चाहिए?
clearEnglish:
Arjuna sharpens the conflict he raised in the previous verse. He says that living on alms would seem better than killing eminent teachers, and that any wealth or enjoyment gained by killing them would feel stained with their blood. The image is not a literal account of what he has already done; it gives voice to his expectation that victory would bring a moral burden rather than uncomplicated happiness.

The verse keeps two concerns in view: the people Arjuna reveres, and the consequences of pursuing material rewards through their deaths. His hesitation is emotionally intense, and it also contains attachment and uncertainty; the text has not yet resolved which consideration should govern his action. We should not turn his anguished statement into a universal instruction to withdraw whenever duty is painful, nor dismiss it as meaningless sentiment. It is a serious moral concern voiced inside a particular epic crisis.

For a modern listener, the image of blood-stained gain invites scrutiny of means as well as outcomes. A promotion, victory, or personal advantage may lose its appeal if obtaining it depends on harming others or betraying important responsibilities. At the same time, when the stakes are high, distress alone does not settle what is right. Careful judgment may require facts, reflection, and the guidance of someone trustworthy.

interpretationPerspectives.label: TEXT
interpretationPerspectives.explanation: Arjuna says that living on alms seems preferable to killing the revered teachers, and imagines that enjoying wealth and desires after killing them would be like enjoying things stained with blood.

interpretationPerspectives.label: DLS translation
interpretationPerspectives.explanation: The Divine Life Society edition renders the first thought as accepting alms rather than slaying the noble teachers, and the later enjoyments as stained with their blood. This conveys the ethical force of the image; the exact local-corpus transliteration is preserved above rather than substituted with the edition's different Roman spelling.

interpretationPerspectives.label: INFERENCE
interpretationPerspectives.explanation: The verse invites reflection on whether an apparent gain can be morally compromised by the harm involved in obtaining it. That is a present-day application, not a separate command spoken in the verse.

practicalApplication.label: Examine the means
practicalApplication.text: Before pursuing an important advantage, ask who could be harmed by the way you seek it, and whether the outcome would still feel worthwhile if those costs were visible.

practicalApplication.label: Seek perspective
practicalApplication.text: When compassion, attachment, and responsibility pull in different directions, write down the concrete facts and talk with a thoughtful, trustworthy person before treating your first emotional response as a final answer.

reflectionQuestion: Is there a gain I am pursuing whose cost to another person deserves more honest attention?
reflectionQuestionHindi: क्या मैं किसी ऐसे लाभ के पीछे हूँ जिसकी किसी दूसरे व्यक्ति पर पड़ने वाली कीमत पर मुझे और ईमानदारी से विचार करना चाहिए?
